segments.english: Ben Zoma says: Who is wise? One who learns from every person, as it is said: "From all my teachers I have gained insight, for Your testimonies are my meditation." Who is mighty? One who subdues his impulse, as it is said: "Better is one slow to anger than a mighty man, and one who rules his spirit than one who captures a city." Who is rich? One who rejoices in his portion, as it is said: "When you eat the toil of your hands, happy are you, and it is well with you." "Happy are you": in this world. "And it is well with you": in the world to come. Who is honored? One who honors people, as it is said: "For those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me will be lightly esteemed."

grammar: The saying has four parallel questions, each introduced by אֵיזֶהוּ ('who is it that...?') and answered by a participle with the article (הַלּוֹמֵד, הַכּוֹבֵשׁ, הַשָּׂמֵחַ, הַמְכַבֵּד): 'the one who learns', 'the one who subdues'. The participle with the article serves as a relative clause.

Each answer is closed by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ('as it is said') and a verse from the Bible; the verses are quoted in their biblical form, so Psalm 119 and 128 address God and the hearer directly, with biblical forms (עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ, לָךְ with 2nd feminine ending) that are not mishnaic Hebrew.

Proverbs 16:32 is built on מִ of comparison, doubled: טוֹב אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם מִגִּבּוֹר וּמֹשֵׁל בְּרוּחוֹ מִלֹּכֵד עִיר, 'better the slow-of-anger than the hero, and the ruler over his spirit than the taker of a city'.

Psalm 128:2: אַשְׁרֶיךָ is a plural construct noun used as an exclamation ('happy are you'). The mishnah splits the verse in two and gives a time to each half: 'in this world' for אַשְׁרֶיךָ and 'in the world to come' for טוֹב לָךְ.

1 Samuel 2:30 pairs a Piel participle (מְכַבְּדַי) with the matching Piel imperfect (אֲכַבֵּד); the verb root כבד has the sense 'be heavy' and the Piel 'give weight to, honor'. The same root underlies מְכֻבָּד (Pual), 'honored'. יֵקָלּוּ 'will be light' is the opposite of 'heavy'.
segments.note: The four questions are answered with the verb in a participle; I kept the form 'One who...' so that each answer stays as brief as the Hebrew. 'Impulse' for יֵצֶר: the inclination of a person's mind and desires, neither good nor evil by the word alone. 'Honored' (מְכֻבָּד) is passive: honored by others, not 'honorable'. Bartenura's reading of מִלֹּכֵד עִיר (see commentary entry 4:1:5) takes the min as 'coming from', and I record it. The Psalm's 'happy are you' and 'well with you' have no verb in Hebrew, and the English likewise has none for 'it is well'.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: since he did not live long and was not ordained to be called 'Rabbi', they called him by his father's name, as with Ben Azzai; both were named Shimon. The English keeps Ben Zoma as a name.

Bartenura: 'so he says: who is wise, such that it is fitting for him to be praised for his wisdom?' The question asks who deserves the title, not who has knowledge; the English keeps the plain question.

Bartenura: 'even if he is smaller than he'; since he does not spare his honor and learns from the young, it is clear that his wisdom is for the sake of Heaven and not to be proud. 'Every person' therefore includes those lesser than oneself.

Bartenura: the end of the verse, כִּי עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ שִׂיחָה לִי, means 'I learned Torah from all my teachers, even the younger ones, without regard for my honor, because my whole intention was for Heaven alone'; similarly the one who is fit to boast of his heroism is the one who subdues his impulse.

Bartenura: the verse means 'better is the patience that comes from the heroism of conquering the impulse, not from a soft nature'; and 'one who rules his spirit' when 'he comes from capturing a city', the king who has taken the city and the men who rebelled are in his hand, yet rules his spirit and does not kill them. This reads the min as 'coming from', not as comparison; the English keeps the comparison of the verse.
Bartenura: the one for whom it is fitting to boast of his wealth is the one who rejoices in his portion.

Bartenura: the three good things named so far, wisdom, might and wealth, make the one who has them honored in the eyes of God and man by himself; so the tanna joins this: he who has these traits and is honored in himself, what shall he do to be honored by others? Let him honor people. It explains why the fourth saying follows; it does not change the words.
Bartenura: an a fortiori argument: if the Holy One, who is the King of Glory and created all things only for His glory, honors those who honor Him, how much more flesh and blood.

Bartenura: we learn the humility of the Holy One; He does not say 'those who despise Me I will curse' but 'they will be lightly esteemed' of themselves (the passive); and He is more strict over the honor of the righteous, as in Gen 12:3 וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ אָאֹר.
Rambam on הַזֶּה: 'this is clear, and we already explained its sense in the preceding chapters' (the contrast between this world and the world to come); nothing to add to the English.

Rabbeinu Yonah: an 'arekh appayim' is one who holds back his anger and waits for a time and place to take revenge; one who rules his spirit is greater, since he forgives from fear of God. A moral gloss, not a reading of the words.

apparatus: Ps 119:99 (Vilna adds the verse number צט): מִכָּל מְלַמְּדַי הִשְׂכַּלְתִּי כִּי עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ שִׂיחָה לִּי.

Spelling variants of Vilna: ומושל (4:1.31), מלוכד (4:1.33), מכובד (4:1.57), ובוזי (4:1.68). Vilna has no text at 4:1.15-18, where the base has כִּי עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ שִׂיחָה לִּי, the second half of the Psalm 119 citation.

grammar: הֱוֵי is an imperative of 'be' (an Aramaic-style form common in the sayings); with the participle רָץ it means 'be running', i.e. 'run'. The two commands are parallel: 'run to...' and 'flee from...' (בּוֹרֵחַ is also a participle).
קַלָּה and חֲמוּרָה are feminine adjectives agreeing with מִצְוָה; the second is used alone with כְּ + בְּ: 'as to a weighty one'.

The reasons are three parallel clauses with שֶׁ, each short: 'a commandment draws a commandment', 'a transgression draws a transgression', and 'the reward of X is X'. The sentences have no verb 'is'; the two nouns are placed side by side.
גּוֹרֶרֶת is a feminine participle of גרר, literally 'drag' (Jastrow 3), here 'draw along, bring after it'.
segments.note: שְׂכַר is 'reward' (wages), and the saying is left as brief as the Hebrew: the reward of a commandment is a commandment. The ambiguity is kept: either the result is another commandment given to the doer (Bartenura's first reading) or the pleasure taken in the act is counted as a commandment (his second). I did not choose between them in the English.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: it is the way of the world that one who has done one commandment finds it easy to do others, and one who starts on transgressions finds it hard to leave them; also, Heaven helps and arranges that he who has done one commandment does another, in order to give him reward for both. Another explanation: whatever pleasure a man takes in doing a commandment is counted as a commandment of its own, and he takes reward for the commandment and for the pleasure he enjoyed in doing it.

Bartenura: the gain and enjoyment that come to a man in doing the transgression is counted as a transgression in itself; he is punished for the transgression and for the profit and enjoyment he received. This is the second explanation of the two sayings on reward; the English keeps the plain saying, which can be read either way.

Rambam refers to his explanation in Sanhedrin ch. 10 and gives the example of Moses, who set apart three cities across the Jordan though they did not yet take effect: 'since a commandment came to my hand, I will do it'. An illustration of the first clause, not a reading of the words.

grammar: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: the personal pronoun with the perfect of 'be' and a participle gives the habitual past, 'he used to say'. The 'he' is the same sage as in 4:2 (Ben Azzai), since no new name is given.
Two parallel prohibitions with אַל and the jussive תְּהִי + a predicate (בָז; מַפְלִיג, a Hiphil participle). Both are followed by לְכָל, 'of any'.
The reason has the idiom שֶׁאֵין לְךָ X שֶׁאֵין לוֹ Y, 'there is no X that has no Y': the 'to you' (לְךָ) is not translated; literally 'for you have no person who has not his hour'.
The word מָקוֹם 'place' is a different word from the divine name הַמָּקוֹם in the decisions; here it means 'a place, a role'.
segments.note: מַפְלִיג has several senses in Jastrow (put off, go too far, speak indefinitely, reject). Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah gloss it as 'regards as distant, far-fetched': 'it is far off that it will happen, no need to worry', so I chose 'dismiss as remote'. Another reading, 'speak too lightly of anything', would also fit the Hebrew, and I did not use it. שָׁעָה 'hour' is a short time, the moment when a person (or thing) counts, as the commentators say: a time when he can harm or help.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: 'to say, what can so-and-so do to harm me?' Contempt for a person is the belief that he can do no harm.
Bartenura: מַפְלִיג is 'keeps at a distance' (מַרְחִיק) regarding every matter about which one should be careful: do not say 'it is far off that it will be, and there is nothing to worry about'.
Rambam: it is impossible that there is not for every person a time when he can harm or benefit, even in a small thing.
Rabbeinu Yonah: 'that he can harm or benefit, a little or a lot': the hour is a time of power to do either.

segments.english: Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh says: Be very, very humble of spirit, for the hope of man is the worm. Rabbi Yohanan son of Beroka says: Whoever profanes the name of Heaven in secret, payment is exacted from him in the open. Whether unwitting or willful, in profaning the Name.

grammar: רַבִּי is 'my master' with the pronominal suffix frozen into the title; אִישׁ יַבְנֶה is 'man of Yavneh', here 'of Yavneh'. The Latin name לְוִיטָס is Levitas.

מְאֹד מְאֹד הֱוֵי שְׁפַל רוּחַ: the repeated adverb stands before the imperative. שְׁפַל רוּחַ is a construct chain with an adjective, 'low of spirit'. The reason שֶׁתִּקְוַת אֱנוֹשׁ רִמָּה has no verb: 'the hope of man (is) the worm'.

כָּל הַמְחַלֵּל ... נִפְרָעִין מִמֶּנּוּ: a casus pendens. The subject is stated first ('whoever profanes...') and then picked up by the pronoun on מִמֶּנּוּ. נִפְרָעִין is an impersonal Nifal participle plural, 'they exact payment' in the passive.
אֶחָד שׁוֹגֵג וְאֶחָד מֵזִיד: the pattern 'one X and one Y' means 'X and Y alike', with the predicate unspoken. בְּחִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם gives the context, 'in the case of profaning the Name'.
segments.note: תִּקְוַת אֱנוֹשׁ: 'the hope of man' can mean 'what man hopes for in the end' (the worm) or 'the expectation of man is for the worm'; Rabbeinu Yonah reads the end of man as the worm, which is the sense kept. For אֶחָד שׁוֹגֵג וְאֶחָד מֵזִיד I kept the ellipsis; Rambam (4:4:2) explains that in both cases payment is exacted openly, each for its own kind of offense, so the pair is 'alike' as to the open exaction, not as to the amount. 'The Name' is the divine name, as in 'profaning the Name'.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: although in other traits the middle way is praised, pride is different; one should lean to the extreme of humility, because pride is most detestable and most people stumble in it; so make an extra distance from it. This is why the doubled מְאֹד.

Rambam: humility is a middle trait between pride and lowness of spirit, but for pride alone the pious went to the opposite extreme; hence the sage said 'very, very be low of spirit', 'because the end of the body is the worm'. The English keeps the extreme.

Rambam: the unwitting has sin, so it needs atonement by a sacrifice, but is not like the willful; the meaning of the mishnah is that for profaning the Name, whether unwitting or willful, payment is exacted in the open: the punishment of the willful for the willful, of the unwitting for the unwitting, but both punishments are open.
Rabbeinu Yonah: not that they exact payment for the unwitting as for the willful, but even for the unwitting they exact payment openly, each according to his sin.

apparatus: No biblical quotation in this mishnah.
No variants are noted in the pack for this mishnah. Rabbeinu Yonah (4:4:4-5) reads 'in secret' as profaning the Name by an act that is itself a profanation, such as a false oath.

segments.english: Rabbi Ishmael, his son, says: One who learns Torah in order to teach, they enable him to learn and to teach. And one who learns in order to do, they enable him to learn and to teach, to keep and to do. Rabbi Zadok says: Do not make them a crown to exalt yourself with, nor a spade to dig with. And thus Hillel used to say: "And he who makes use of the crown passes away." Hence you have learned: whoever derives benefit from the words of Torah takes his life from the world.

whoever derives benefit from the words of Torah

phrases.literal: 'from the-world'; Rambam: from the life of the world to come

grammar: The first two sayings are in parallel: הַלּוֹמֵד עַל מְנָת לְ... מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ ...; the subject is a participle with the article, the verb is an impersonal plural participle (מַסְפִּיקִין, 'they enable'), and the aims are infinitives with לְ. The second saying adds 'to keep and to do'.

אַל תַּעֲשֵׂם ... וְלֹא קַרְדֹּם: a prohibition with אַל and the imperfect; the second clause, with וְלֹא, takes its verb from the first ('nor (make them) a spade'). The suffix -ם 'them' stands for the words of the Torah, to which the prior saying referred.

Hillel's saying וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּתָגָא חָלָף is in Aramaic: the relative דְּ, the Ithpaal perfect אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ, תָּגָא 'crown' with the Aramaic ending -ā, and the verb at the end. Rabbeinu Yonah notes 'tagā means crown, as in the Targum'.

הָא לָמַדְתָּ ('behold, you have learned') introduces the conclusion drawn by the editor from Hillel's saying; כָּל הַנֶּהֱנֶה is again 'whoever + participle'. נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם is a participle, the present of a general rule: 'takes his life out of the world'.
The word חַיָּיו is plural in form (חַיִּים 'life') and has a singular sense; מִן הָעוֹלָם 'from the world' needs the world to come in the Rambam's reading.
segments.note: עַל מְנָת: 'in order to, with the intention of' (literally 'on the portion of'). The mishnah's first two sayings are about intent: in each case the aim of the learning decides what he is enabled to do. The reading 'they enable' is Bartenura's majority text; he records another text, 'one who learns in order to teach, they do not enable him to learn and to teach', for those who take 'to teach' as 'in order to be called Rabbi'; I follow the majority text. קַרְדֹּם is 'spade' (the tool named with לַחְפֹּר 'to dig'); Rabbeinu Yonah's variant 'to cut' (לַחְתֹּךְ) would make it an axe. נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם: Rambam says 'his life from the world', i.e. from the life of the world to come; I kept the literal words and give the gloss here.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: 'we read': one who learns in order always to be occupied with Torah, with no intention to do acts of kindness, they enable his intention to be done, to learn and to teach; one who learns in order to do, wanting to be occupied with Torah and also to do kindness, they enable him to complete his intention and he merits to learn, teach, keep and do. Some explain 'to teach' as 'to be called Rabbi' and read 'they do not enable him'; but in most books he found the first reading, which is the main one.
Bartenura: 'so that you do not say, I will learn so that I be called Rabbi and they seat me at the head, but learn from love, and in the end honor will come.'

Bartenura: do not learn Torah to make from it a trade by which to live, like a spade to dig with; whoever does so misuses the holiness of the Torah and is liable to death at the hands of Heaven, like one who benefits from the Temple's consecrated property. Teachers of children take only the wages of watching the children and of teaching the cantillation, not for teaching itself.

Rambam: 'do not make the Torah a spade to dig with' means do not regard it as an instrument to live by; he who benefits in this world from the honor of the Torah 'takes his life from the world', that is, from the life of the world to come. He devotes a long defense of sages who lived by a trade, not by the community's money, and tells the story of R. Tarfon.
Rabbeinu Yonah: 'tagā is a word for a crown, as its Targum.'

apparatus: Rabbeinu Yonah (4:5:1) says the copyist's text before him reads 'Rabbi Ishmael'; the base text of some versions has 'Rabbi Shimon his son': the pack's commentary records this alternative name.

Vilna spelling variants: ללמוד (4:5.12, 4:5.20), לשמור (4:5.22), קרדום (4:5.33), לחפור (4:5.34), ודישתמש (4:5.40, for the base וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ); the pack also shows that Vilna has no word at 4:5.6 where the base has תּוֹרָה.
Bartenura's variant text: 'one who learns in order to teach: they do not enable him to learn and to teach' (taking לְלַמֵּד as 'in order to be called Rabbi'); he follows the reading in most books.

'upon the-creatures': 'upon' here marks the persons in whose view he is honored

grammar: Two antithetical sayings, one with מְכַבֵּד / מְכֻבָּד (root כבד, Piel / Pual) and one with מְחַלֵּל / מְחֻלָּל (root חלל, Piel / Pual). In each, the Piel participle with the article after כָּל is the subject, and the Pual participle is the predicate of the main clause (a casus pendens: 'whoever honors..., his body is honored').
The two verbs are opposites: כבד 'give weight to', חלל 'treat as common, make profane'. The second saying keeps the same word order to make the contrast plain.
עַל הַבְּרִיּוֹת, literally 'upon the creatures', stands for the agent: 'honored by people', 'in the eyes of people'. The word גּוּף 'body' with the suffix is a way to say 'he himself, his person'.
The verb חִלֵּל is the same as in 4:4 (חִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם): to profane the Name and to profane the Torah are both 'make common'.
segments.note: גּוּפוֹ is 'his body' in the Hebrew, and I kept it, though it can be read as 'he himself'; Rabbeinu Yonah explains that Heaven helps people to honor him (or to despise him), i.e. 'body' is the person in the eyes of others. 'By people' for עַל הַבְּרִיּוֹת: literally 'upon the creatures', the persons in whose eyes the honor is held.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: one who expounds the extra and missing letters of the Torah and shows a reason for every point, saying nothing in it is superfluous, no greater honor to the Torah; or one who honors a Torah scroll and those who learn and engage in it; all these are 'one who honors the Torah'.
Rambam: the honor of the Torah is shown by zeal in doing it, and by honoring the sages who uphold it and the books they wrote on it; and the profaning of the Torah is the opposite.

apparatus: No biblical quotation in this mishnah.
Vilna spelling variants: מכובד (4:6.9), מחולל (4:6.17), for the base's מְכֻבָּד and מְחֻלָּל.
